issues.legal_issue: A court may draw an adverse inference from a party’s failure to appear as a witness only when there is no other evidence on the point in issue.
material_facts: In an execution proceeding, the creditor sought to rely on the absence of the secured creditor and purchaser from the witness box.
The record contained the creditor’s admission, the judgment-debtor’s statement, and documents concerning the secured debt and the sale of the attached property.
issues.conclusion: Because evidence on the disputed point was already on the record, the parties’ absence from the witness box did not justify drawing an adverse inference against them.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 114 of the Evidence Act, an adverse inference based on a party’s failure to appear in court arises only when there is no other evidence on the point in issue. The Court cited no earlier cases for this proposition.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The dispute arose in proceedings to enforce a court decree.
predicates.party_did_not_testify: A party whose conduct was in issue did not appear as a witness.
predicates.evidence_on_disputed_point_exists: Other evidence in the record addressed the point on which an inference was sought.

issues.definition: When enforcement proceedings involve a party who did not testify but the record contains other evidence on the disputed point, the absence alone does not justify an adverse inference.

issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may not reverse concurrent factual findings merely by reappraising evidence that supports those findings.
material_facts: The executing court and the District Judge both found that the property had been pledged, had been sold by the pledgee, and remained subject to the pledgee’s unpaid debt.
The High Court, exercising Letters Patent appellate jurisdiction after a second appeal, reassessed the evidence and reversed those concurrent findings.
The findings below rested on the creditor’s admission, the judgment-debtor’s statement, and documentary evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by reversing the concurrent findings on the record before it; the Supreme Court set aside its judgment and restored the District Judge’s decree.
issues.legal_principle: Concurrent factual findings supported by evidence are not normally to be set aside by a second appellate court through a fresh appraisal of the evidence. The Court cited no specific provision or earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and record_supports_findings and appellate_court_reappraises_evidence

predicates.second_appeal: The matter reached the appellate court in a proceeding following a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: Two lower courts made the same findings of fact.
predicates.record_supports_findings: Evidence in the record supports the findings made by the lower courts.
predicates.appellate_court_reappraises_evidence: The appellate court reassesses the evidence to reach different factual findings.

issues.definition: When a court hearing a matter following a second appeal reappraises evidence supporting factual findings shared by two lower courts, reversing those findings exceeds its appellate jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A decree-holder cannot compel production of pledged property or its sale proceeds while the pledgee’s secured debt remains unpaid and the attachment is subject to the pledge.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor had pledged the property to the secured creditor, and the creditor knew of the secured debt and had agreed that the debt would be paid before his own dues.
The attachment was subject to the secured creditor’s lien.
The pledgee sold the property to a purchaser, but the sale did not satisfy the pledgee’s debt.
The decree-holder sought to compel the pledgee or purchaser to produce the property or sale proceeds in the execution proceeding.
issues.conclusion: While the pledgee’s debt remained unpaid, the decree-holder could not compel the pledgee or purchaser to produce the property or its sale proceeds.
issues.legal_principle: Section 176 of the Contract Act recognizes the pledgee’s right to sell pledged property after giving due notice. An attachment subject to an existing pledge does not enable the decree-holder to proceed against the property or its proceeds until the secured debt is satisfied. The Court cited no earlier cases for this principle.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and property_was_pledged and attachment_was_subject_to_prior_lien and secured_debt_remains_unpaid

predicates.execution_proceeding: A decree-holder sought to enforce a decree against property in execution proceedings.
predicates.property_was_pledged: The judgment-debtor had given the property as security to a creditor.
predicates.attachment_was_subject_to_prior_lien: The attachment did not displace the creditor’s existing security interest in the property.
predicates.secured_debt_remains_unpaid: The proceeds of sale or other payment had not fully satisfied the secured creditor’s debt.

issues.definition: In execution proceedings, when attached property remains subject to a pledge and the secured debt is unpaid, the decree-holder cannot compel production of the property or its sale proceeds.
